high-temperature-001.question: Which statement about the three stages of a creep curve (strain versus time) measured at constant load and temperature is correct?
choices: In transient (primary) creep the strain rate increases with time, reaches its constant maximum value in steady-state (secondary) creep, and then keeps decreasing throughout accelerating (tertiary) creep

In transient creep the strain rate gradually decreases, in steady-state creep work hardening and recovery balance so the rate is nearly constant, and in accelerating creep the rate rises until rupture

In the steady-state (secondary) stage, work hardening and recovery balance so that dislocation motion stops completely, and from the end of transient creep until accelerating creep begins the strain does not increase at all
high-temperature-001.explanation: After the instantaneous strain on loading, in transient creep work hardening from multiplying and tangling dislocations outweighs recovery, and the strain rate gradually falls. In steady-state creep, work hardening and recovery by processes such as dislocation climb balance, so the strain rate is at its minimum and nearly constant. This stage occupies most of the life, so design uses the steady-state (minimum) creep rate. In accelerating creep, the nucleation and coalescence of voids on grain boundaries, the loss of cross section by necking and microstructural degradation raise the strain rate until rupture. The description with the rate trends reversed confuses the order of the stages. Steady state means the strain rate is constant, not that the strain stops.

high-temperature-002.question: The steady-state creep rate of a heat-resistant alloy follows the power law ε̇ = Aσⁿexp(−Q/RT) with a stress exponent of n = 5. If the stress is raised by 20% at the same temperature, by roughly what factor does the steady-state creep rate increase?
choices: About 2.5 times
About 6.0 times
About 1.2 times
high-temperature-002.explanation: At the same temperature A and exp(−Q/RT) do not change, so the ratio of the rates is the stress ratio raised to the power n: (1.2)⁵ ≈ 2.49, about 2.5 times. That a mere 20% increase in stress more than doubles the rate is characteristic of dislocation creep (power-law creep), where n is large, about 3 to 8, and a small error in the design stress greatly affects the life. About 6.0 times is the value obtained by multiplying the stress ratio by the exponent n, and about 1.2 times assumes that the rate is proportional to stress (n = 1), which is the case for diffusion creep operating at low stress. Plotting rate against stress on log-log axes gives a slope of n.

high-temperature-003.question: An alloy has a steady-state creep rate that follows ε̇ = Aσⁿexp(−Q/RT) with an activation energy of Q = 300 kJ/mol. If the temperature is raised from 1000 K to 1050 K at the same stress, by roughly what factor does the steady-state creep rate increase? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 1.05 times
About 52 times
About 5.6 times
high-temperature-003.explanation: The ratio of the rates is exp[(Q/R)(1/1000 − 1/1050)]. Since Q/R = 300000/8.314 ≈ 3.61×10⁴ K and (1/1000 − 1/1050) ≈ 4.76×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, the exponent is about 1.72, and exp(1.72) ≈ 5.6 times. A rise of only 50 K increases the rate more than fivefold because the rate depends exponentially on temperature. The activation energy for high-temperature creep of pure metals is often close to that for self-diffusion, showing that creep is controlled by diffusion. About 52 times is the value obtained by treating the natural exponent as a power of 10, and about 1.05 times takes the ratio of the absolute temperatures as the ratio of the rates.

high-temperature-004.question: A fine-grained polycrystalline metal was creep tested at a low stress at about 0.5 times its melting point (in absolute temperature). The steady-state creep rate was nearly proportional to stress (stress exponent n ≈ 1) and nearly inversely proportional to the cube of the grain size. Which creep mechanism is most likely to be operating?
choices: Power-law creep controlled by dislocation climb in the grain interiors
Coble creep by diffusion of atoms along grain boundaries
Nabarro–Herring creep by lattice diffusion through the grain interiors
high-temperature-004.explanation: In diffusion creep, atoms diffuse from grain boundaries under tension to those under compression, elongating the grains, and the rate is proportional to stress (n = 1). When the diffusion path runs along the grain boundaries it is called Coble creep, and the rate is inversely proportional to the cube of the grain size. When it is lattice diffusion through the grain interiors it is called Nabarro–Herring creep, and the rate is inversely proportional to the square of the grain size. Grain boundary diffusion has a lower activation energy than lattice diffusion, so Coble creep dominates at relatively low temperatures and fine grain sizes, while the contribution of Nabarro–Herring creep grows at high temperatures near the melting point. Power-law creep by dislocations has a large n of 3 to 8 and hardly depends on grain size.

high-temperature-005.question: Which statement about the deformation mechanism map of Ashby and coworkers (with stress normalized by the shear modulus, σ/G, on the vertical axis and homologous temperature T/Tm on the horizontal axis) is correct? Tm is the melting point in absolute temperature.
choices: For a fixed grain size, it shows the field of the fastest mechanism at each stress and temperature; diffusion creep lies at low stress and high temperature, and power-law creep at higher stresses
The field of each mechanism is set only by the kind of material, so the boundary between diffusion creep and power-law creep does not move at all whether the grains are refined or coarsened
The field of dislocation glide widens toward lower stresses and higher temperatures, and the diffusion creep field appears only at high stresses close to the ideal strength and at low temperatures
high-temperature-005.explanation: A deformation mechanism map uses the rate equation of each mechanism to find which one deforms the material fastest at a given stress and temperature, and shades its field. Because several mechanisms act in parallel, the fastest one is taken to be dominant. Dislocation glide dominates at high stresses close to the ideal strength, power-law creep involving dislocation climb at intermediate stresses and high temperatures, and diffusion creep at low stresses and high temperatures. Since the rate of diffusion creep is inversely proportional to the square or cube of the grain size, refining the grains enlarges the diffusion creep field, so the boundaries do move. Contours of constant strain rate are also drawn, so the mechanism and the deformation rate under service conditions can be read off. Placing dislocation glide on the low-stress side gets the layout wrong.

high-temperature-006.question: At room temperature, refining the grains raises strength (the Hall–Petch relation), but components loaded for long times at high temperature often use coarse grains or single crystals. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Coarser grains give a higher Young's modulus and so a smaller elastic strain at the same stress, which keeps the creep strain small even under long loading at high temperature

At high temperature grain boundaries become stronger than the grain interiors, so reducing the boundaries keeps dislocations from being stopped too much at them and instead lets dislocation motion in the grains relax the stress

At high temperature grain boundaries become fast diffusion paths and sliding sites, so grain boundary diffusion creep, grain boundary sliding and void formation on boundaries all become easier the more boundaries there are
high-temperature-006.explanation: At high temperature, diffusion of atoms along grain boundaries is fast and grain boundary sliding also occurs, so grain boundaries become weak spots. The temperature at which grain boundaries and grain interiors are equally strong is called the equicohesive temperature, and above it the boundaries are the weaker. Diffusion creep (especially Coble creep, inversely proportional to the cube of grain size), grain boundary sliding, and rupture by the nucleation and coalescence of voids on boundaries therefore occur more readily in fine-grained material with many boundaries. That is why coarse grains, columnar grains parallel to the stress, and even single crystals are used in high-temperature components. Young's modulus is set by interatomic bonding and hardly depends on grain size, so it is no advantage of coarse grains. The statement that boundaries become stronger than the interiors at high temperature reverses the relationship.

high-temperature-007.question: A heat-resistant alloy ruptured by creep in 1000 h at 1000 K under a certain stress. Assuming the Larson–Miller parameter P = T(C + log₁₀t_r) (T is the absolute temperature, t_r is the rupture time in h, and C = 20) is constant at the same stress, which temperature is closest to that giving a rupture life of 10⁵ h at the same stress?
choices: About 920 K
About 854 K
About 600 K
high-temperature-007.explanation: From the test condition, P = 1000 × (20 + log₁₀1000) = 1000 × 23 = 23000. For 10⁵ h, log₁₀t_r = 5, so T = 23000/(20 + 5) = 920 K. Lowering the temperature by only 80 K extends the life a hundredfold, and estimating long lives at lower temperatures from short tests at higher temperatures is what this parameter is used for. About 854 K uses the natural logarithm instead of the common logarithm, and about 600 K forgets the constant C and takes P = T log₁₀t_r. However, if the microstructure changes or the deformation mechanism shifts over long times, the extrapolation fails, so an extrapolation as large as a hundredfold, as in this example, must be treated with care, and the extrapolation range should not be stretched needlessly.

high-temperature-008.question: Which statement about the γ' phase that provides the high-temperature strength of nickel-based superalloys is correct?
choices: It is a BCC (B2-type) ordered phase with a large lattice mismatch and incoherent interfaces with the matrix γ, so it precipitates as coarse particles at grain boundaries and in the grains that strongly pin dislocations
It is Ni₃Al with the L1₂ ordered structure (an ordered phase based on FCC), with nearly the same lattice parameter as the matrix γ, and precipitates finely with coherent interfaces

It is a carbide such as M₂₃C₆ that precipitates as a continuous film on grain boundaries; the more of it there is, the better grain boundary sliding is stopped and the higher both ductility and creep strength become
high-temperature-008.explanation: The γ' phase is an L1₂ ordered phase of composition Ni₃(Al,Ti), in which Al occupies the corners and Ni the face centers of the FCC lattice. Its lattice parameter differs little from that of the matrix γ (an FCC Ni solid solution) (small misfit), so fine cuboidal particles precipitate with coherent interfaces, reaching 60 to 70% by volume in alloys for single-crystal blades. When a dislocation in γ enters γ', it disturbs the ordered arrangement and creates an antiphase boundary, so dislocations must travel in pairs, which gives a large resistance. γ' is stable up to high temperatures and also shows an anomalous temperature dependence in which the yield stress rises with temperature up to about 700 to 800 °C. Calling it BCC mistakes the crystal structure, and calling it a grain boundary carbide confuses it with another phase; a film-like carbide is actually a cause of brittleness.

high-temperature-009.question: Why are directionally solidified columnar-grained or single-crystal nickel-based superalloys used for jet engine turbine blades?
choices: Because a single crystal contains no dislocations at all, so creep deformation cannot occur
Because a single crystal allows more carbon and boron, which are used to strengthen grain boundaries, to be added, so the alloy can be strengthened by their carbides and borides

Because removing grain boundaries perpendicular to the stress eliminates the sites where creep damage starts, and a single crystal can do without grain-boundary-strengthening elements, so it can be solution treated at high temperature to make γ' uniform and fine
high-temperature-009.explanation: Turbine blades are pulled along their length by centrifugal force, and grain boundaries perpendicular to the stress become the starting points of creep voids and cracks. Directional solidification produces columnar grains aligned with the stress, removing the perpendicular boundaries. In single-crystal blades, grown so that only one crystal is selected, there are no grain boundaries at all. When C, B, Zr and other grain-boundary strengtheners are no longer needed, the temperature at which the alloy begins to melt rises, so solution treatment can be done at high temperature to dissolve γ' fully and then reprecipitate it uniformly and finely. The statement about adding more strengtheners reverses this relationship. Single crystals still contain dislocations, and creep proceeds by their motion within the crystal.

high-temperature-010.question: What is the main purpose of adding a few percent of heavy elements such as rhenium (Re) to single-crystal nickel-based superalloys?
choices: To dissolve in the γ matrix and slow diffusion, giving solid-solution strengthening and slower γ' coarsening, and so raise creep strength at high temperature
To form on the surface a dense film of rhenium oxide that hardly volatilizes, raising the oxidation resistance at high temperatures in place of the Al₂O₃ film
To lower the alloy's density, reducing the centrifugal stress on the fast-rotating blade and so extending the creep rupture life at the same temperature
high-temperature-010.explanation: Re is an element that diffuses very slowly in the alloy and partitions mainly to the γ matrix, where it dissolves. Besides solid-solution strengthening of γ, it slows the coarsening of γ' and rafting, in which γ' joins into plates under stress at high temperature, greatly raising creep strength. Generations of single-crystal alloys are sometimes distinguished by their Re content, such as second-generation alloys with about 3% Re and third-generation alloys with about 6%. However, too much Re makes brittle TCP phases such as the σ phase likely to precipitate. Re is a heavy element, so it raises rather than lowers the density, and its oxide is volatile and does not form a protective film. Oxidation resistance is provided mainly by the Al₂O₃ film formed by Al.

high-temperature-011.question: When an alloy was oxidized in air at high temperature, it followed the parabolic law x² = k_p t, in which diffusion through the dense oxide scale controls the rate, and the scale was 2.0 µm thick after 100 h. Which is closest to the scale thickness after 900 h of oxidation at the same temperature?
choices: About 18 µm
About 6.0 µm
About 4.2 µm
high-temperature-011.explanation: Under the parabolic law the thickness is proportional to the square root of time, so x = 2.0 × √(900/100) = 2.0 × 3 = 6.0 µm. As the scale thickens, the distance that ions and electrons must travel through it grows and growth slows, giving this form (Wagner's theory). About 18 µm is calculated with the linear law, in which thickness is proportional to time; the linear law is seen when the scale is porous or cracked and not protective, or when a reaction at an interface controls the rate. About 4.2 µm is calculated with the cubic law, in which thickness is proportional to the cube root of time. The smaller the parabolic rate constant k_p of a scale, the more protective it is, and this serves as a guide in choosing alloys.

high-temperature-012.question: The Pilling–Bedworth ratio of a metal's oxide scale (PBR, the ratio of the volume of oxide to the volume of metal used to form it) is calculated as PBR = (M_ox ρ_M)/(n M_M ρ_ox) (M is the molar mass, ρ is the density, and n is the number of metal atoms in one formula unit of the oxide). For magnesium (24.31 g/mol, 1.74 g/cm³) and MgO (40.30 g/mol, 3.58 g/cm³, n = 1), which combination of PBR and scale behavior is correct?
choices: About 1.24, so the scale is under moderate compressive stress and forms a protective film covering the metal
About 0.81, and because it is less than 1 the scale shrinks into a dense layer that protects the metal well
About 0.81, so the scale cannot fully cover the metal surface, cracks easily and is unlikely to be protective
high-temperature-012.explanation: PBR = (40.30 × 1.74)/(1 × 24.31 × 3.58) = 70.1/87.0 ≈ 0.81. When the PBR is less than 1, the volume of oxide is smaller than the volume of metal consumed, so the scale is under tensile stress and cracks or develops gaps, letting oxygen reach the metal easily. Around 1 to 2, the scale tends to cover the metal without gaps and to be protective, as with aluminum forming Al₂O₃ (PBR ≈ 1.29), whereas well above 2 the compressive stress becomes too large and the scale tends to spall. About 1.24 is the value with numerator and denominator swapped. The PBR is only a guide; protectiveness also depends on the rate of diffusion through the scale and its adhesion.

high-temperature-013.question: Which statement about the protective scales on heat-resistant alloys used in air at high temperatures above 1000 °C is correct?
choices: A Cr₂O₃ scale does not volatilize at any temperature, so above 1000 °C it is always more protective than an Al₂O₃ scale
A Cr₂O₃ scale tends to be lost as volatile CrO₃ above about 1000 °C, so at higher temperatures alloys that form an Al₂O₃ scale are used
The faster and thicker a scale grows, the more protective it is, so choose alloys forming oxides with a large parabolic rate constant
high-temperature-013.explanation: A protective scale at high temperature must be dense, have slow diffusion through it (a small parabolic rate constant) and adhere well to the substrate; the typical examples are Cr₂O₃, Al₂O₃ and SiO₂. Cr₂O₃ is a good protective scale up to about 1000 °C, but at higher temperatures in oxidizing atmospheres it forms gaseous CrO₃ and volatilizes, thinning the scale. Al₂O₃ grows even more slowly and is stable to high temperatures, so nickel-based superalloys, bond coats of thermal barrier coatings and Fe-Cr-Al heating elements are made to form Al₂O₃. Adding small amounts of Y or Hf improves the adhesion of the scale (the reactive element effect). A scale that grows fast and thick means the metal is consumed fast, which is the opposite of being protective.

high-temperature-014.question: Which statement about the structure of a thermal barrier coating (TBC) applied to gas turbine blades is correct?
choices: Beneath a low-conductivity zirconia (YSZ) top coat lies a bond coat such as MCrAlY, and a thin Al₂O₃ thermally grown oxide (TGO) forming at their interface protects the substrate from oxidation
The top coat is dense, highly conductive alumina that quickly carries heat out of the blade to cool the metal, while the bond coat absorbs the thermal expansion mismatch with the substrate
The YSZ top coat lets no oxygen through at all, so no bond coat is needed, and YSZ sprayed directly onto the substrate blocks both oxidation and heat
high-temperature-014.explanation: A TBC is a coating that lowers the metal temperature with an insulating surface layer while the inside of the blade is cooled by cooling air. The YSZ (yttria partially stabilized zirconia) top coat has a low thermal conductivity of about 1 to 2 W/(m·K) and, for a ceramic, a large thermal expansion coefficient. It is made as a porous sprayed coating or a columnar vapor-deposited coating to relieve the strain from the thermal expansion mismatch with the substrate. YSZ conducts oxide ions well and cannot stop oxygen, so Al in the bond coat oxidizes to form a thin Al₂O₃ TGO, which protects the substrate from oxidation. When the TGO thickens or undergoes thermal cycling, the top coat spalls from near it, which is the main factor limiting the life. A material with high thermal conductivity cannot serve as insulation.

high-temperature-015.question: A heat flux of 1.0 MW/m² passes uniformly through the thickness of the top coat of a thermal barrier coating (thickness 250 µm, thermal conductivity 1.2 W/(m·K)). Treating it as steady one-dimensional heat conduction, which is closest to the temperature difference between the two faces of the top coat?
choices: About 300 K
About 21 K
About 208 K
high-temperature-015.explanation: From Fourier's law q = kΔT/L, ΔT = qL/k = (1.0×10⁶ × 250×10⁻⁶)/1.2 ≈ 208 K. That a coating only about 0.25 mm thick can lower the metal temperature by about 200 K is the benefit of a thermal barrier coating. The creep strength of nickel-based superalloys is sensitive to temperature, so this temperature difference strongly affects the life and the allowable gas temperature. About 300 K multiplies by the thermal conductivity instead of dividing, and about 21 K converts the thickness as 25 µm, an order of magnitude too small. The lower the thermal conductivity and the thicker the coating, the larger the temperature difference, but thicker coatings spall more easily under thermal stress, so the thickness is limited.
